slides.heading: How CRISPR Is Revolutionizing Medicine
slides.body: The gene-editing breakthrough transforming how we treat genetic disease, cancer, and more

slides.heading: What Is CRISPR?
slides.body: CRISPR-Cas9 is a molecular tool that acts like genetic scissors. It can find a specific sequence in DNA and precisely cut it, allowing scientists to disable, repair, or replace genes with extraordinary accuracy.

slides.heading: Inspired by Bacteria
slides.body: CRISPR was discovered in bacteria, which naturally use it to remember and destroy viruses. Scientists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier adapted this defense system into a programmable editing tool, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

slides.heading: Sickle Cell Disease: A Cure Achieved
slides.body: In 2023, the FDA approved the first CRISPR-based therapy — Casgevy — for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia. Patients who once needed regular transfusions are now living symptom-free after a single treatment.

slides.heading: Taking On Cancer
slides.body: Researchers are engineering patients' own immune T-cells with CRISPR to make them better hunters of tumor cells. Early clinical trials show promising results for leukemia and other blood cancers that resisted conventional therapies.

slides.heading: Targeting Hereditary Blindness
slides.body: CRISPR therapies delivered directly into the eye are restoring vision for people with Leber congenital amaurosis, a rare inherited blindness. This marks the first in-body (in vivo) CRISPR editing in human patients.

slides.heading: Lowering Cholesterol Permanently
slides.body: A single CRISPR injection can silence the PCSK9 gene in liver cells, causing LDL cholesterol to drop by up to 60% — potentially for life. This could replace daily statin pills for millions of people at high cardiovascular risk.

slides.heading: The Risks and Ethical Debates
slides.body: Off-target edits — cuts in the wrong DNA location — remain a safety concern. The 2018 case of gene-edited babies in China sparked global outrage and led to international calls for strict ethical oversight of germline editing.

slides.heading: Next Generation: Base & Prime Editing
slides.body: Newer tools like base editing and prime editing offer even more precision — making single-letter DNA corrections without cutting the double helix. They dramatically reduce off-target effects and open doors to hundreds more treatable conditions.

slides.heading: The Future of Genetic Medicine
slides.body: CRISPR has moved from lab curiosity to approved therapy in under a decade. As delivery methods improve and costs fall, personalized gene correction could become as routine as surgery — rewriting the story of inherited disease forever.
